overview: This file consists of twelve consecutive State Department “List of Papers” register sheets summarizing documents numbered roughly 224–286, principally from 1939–1942, concerning wireless telegraphy and shortwave broadcasting involving Japan. Most entries trace complaints about Japanese and other Asian stations interfering with American commercial, press, and naval radio services—especially KGEI at San Francisco, naval station NSS, direction-finding services, and Press Wireless station WJS—and the diplomatic representations made through the American Embassy in Tokyo. The register also records reception reports from China and the Netherlands East Indies, discussions of program content, translated Japanese broadcasts, and, after the United States entered the war, proposals to jam Japanese broadcasts directed toward Brazil and Latin America.

subfiles.title: Register entries on KGEI, KJY, and Asian interference
subfiles.about: This register page indexes early complaints about interference with American broadcasts in East and Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Entries cover the apparent cessation of interference with KJY, reports from Batavia about KGEI reception, and Japan’s assertion that station JZI possessed frequency priority. The State Department informed the Federal Communications Commission and General Electric that it could not readily insist on KGEI’s priority over Japanese and Hong Kong stations, while also pursuing interference attributed to a Bangkok station. One indexed Batavia report dates from November 1939, although most entries are from January 1940.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 41: KGEI and NSS complaints
subfiles.about: The sheet records January 1940 correspondence about interference affecting KGEI and naval radio station NSS.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanked Dickover for his Batavia reception study and instructed Neville to approach Thai authorities about station HSSPJ. Grew reported that repeated discussions with the Japanese Foreign Office had not resolved interference with NSS. The Federal Communications Commission disputed the Department’s doubts about KGEI’s priority over JZI and Hong Kong station ZBW-3, and the sheet also indexes a Japanese Foreign Office reply on the KGEI dispute.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 42: February 1940 interference cases
subfiles.about: This sheet indexes February 1940 reports and instructions concerning Japanese interference with American naval and commercial stations.
subfiles.summary: Japan requested technical details about JND’s interference with NSS, while the Navy reported no improvement and the Department ordered renewed representations. Other entries concern alleged JDK interference with KJY in the Philippines and complaints from American listeners in Peiping about JZI’s disruption of KGEI. An internal memorandum and correspondence with the Federal Communications Commission discuss registration priority and the lack of a suitable alternative frequency for KGEI.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 43: technical and diplomatic remedies
subfiles.about: The sheet records proposed technical remedies and diplomatic action concerning KGEI, NSS, and naval direction-finding interference.
subfiles.summary: The Federal Communications Commission maintained that the United States had priority on 9530 kilocycles but worked with General Electric on temporary solutions, including greater transmitter power and shared frequencies. Navy reports supplied further details about JND’s continued interference with NSS. Separate entries address Japanese vessels disrupting the Naval Communication System’s direction-finding service on 375 kilocycles and instructions to press Tokyo for immediate relief.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 44: Japanese responses and Thai frequencies
subfiles.about: This sheet indexes March–April 1940 diplomatic exchanges on Japanese radio interference and a Thai investigation of alleged interference with KGEI.
subfiles.summary: Grew reported repeated approaches to the Japanese Foreign Office about JND interference with naval communications and relayed Japanese promises of action. Further entries concern Japanese inter-ship messages affecting U.S. Navy direction finding and the circulation of Tokyo’s replies to the Navy. Neville reported that none of Thailand’s listed stations could be responsible for the interference alleged on 9510 kilocycles, while Johnson reported clear KGEI reception at Chongqing and recommended more American news content.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 45: KGEI reception and embassy enclosures
subfiles.about: The page records follow-up correspondence on Thai interference, KGEI programming, and Japanese replies regarding naval communications.
subfiles.summary: The Federal Communications Commission noted that Thai station HSBPJ had become HSP6, and Batavia was asked whether interference had ended locally. General Electric and the Commission acknowledged correspondence about KGEI reception and Johnson’s request for different news content. Grew’s despatches transmitting the Embassy’s notes and Japanese Foreign Office replies on JND and naval direction-finding interference were forwarded to the Navy.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 46: Shanghai complaints and KJY follow-up
subfiles.about: This register sheet covers Japanese reports on naval interference and American broadcast reception complaints from Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmitted a Japanese Foreign Ministry report on interference with naval direction finding, which was later sent to the Navy. The Commerce Department relayed A. Viola Smith’s Shanghai complaint about Japanese interference with KGEI and summarized the positions of General Electric and the Federal Communications Commission. Japan denied that JDK could be interfering with KJY, and the Commission later reported that no such interference had been observed for several months; General Electric also forwarded letters praising American news broadcasts.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 47: naval cases and Press Wireless station WJS
subfiles.about: The sheet concludes earlier naval interference cases and opens a new dispute involving Japanese interference with Press Wireless station WJS.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmitted Japanese Foreign Ministry communications concerning JND interference with NSS and JDK interference with KJY. Later entries show the Federal Communications Commission asking the Department to stop station JZP from interfering with WJS. The Embassy approached Japanese authorities, who attributed the problem to inadvertent frequency use in communications with Australia and New Zealand and suggested it had already been corrected.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 48: continued WJS–JZP interference
subfiles.about: This page indexes the October–November 1940 diplomatic campaign to end Japanese interference with Press Wireless station WJS.
subfiles.summary: The Federal Communications Commission documented continuing interference between October 22 and 31 and requested Japanese cooperation. Grew transmitted Embassy notes and Japanese Foreign Office replies, including the explanation that JZ and JZP were call letters of the same station and that the cause was believed eliminated on October 23. Because interference continued daily, the Department ordered further representations, culminating in an Embassy note verbale of November 22.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 49: broadcasting restrictions and East Asian reception reports
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes a broadcasting restriction in Japan and a series of 1941 reports on the reception and content of American broadcasts in China.
subfiles.summary: Grew reported the temporary exclusion of W. R. Wills from Japanese radio broadcasting and the subsequent removal of the ban. Most later entries concern weak or variable reception of KGEI at Chongqing, Shanghai, and Tianjin, including monitoring logs supplied by American listeners and correspondence with the Federal Communications Commission, Commerce Department, and General Electric. The page also notes Alger Hiss’s memorandum quoting transcripts from Chongqing station XGOY and includes an unrelated cross-reference concerning cobalt shipments through Canada to Japan.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 50: Japanese broadcast transcripts and proposed jamming
subfiles.about: This sheet records translated Tokyo broadcasts and requests to disrupt Japanese shortwave transmissions directed toward Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The Justice Department supplied translated transcripts of broadcasts from Tokyo dating from October through December 1941. A report from Paraguay concerned Japanese broadcasts aimed at Latin America, while the American Consul General at São Paulo sought U.S. help against Tokyo programs transmitted to Brazil in Portuguese and Japanese. The Defense Communications Board referred the matter to appropriate authorities and suggested that Brazilian stations might jam the broadcasts locally.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Page 51: jamming policy and China reception complaint
subfiles.about: The final sheet continues the jamming discussion and records a complaint about interference with an American broadcasting station in China.
subfiles.summary: A March 3 telegram from São Paulo explained why producing interference from within the United States would be inadvisable. A March 16 entry from China, associated in the OCR with Xi’an and Guangxi, reported interference affecting what appears to be station KGEI. The latter entry is highly garbled but indicates that reception would otherwise have been good.

interest: The register is particularly useful for reconstructing the bureaucratic and diplomatic chain through which radio complaints moved among the State Department, Federal Communications Commission, Navy, Commerce Department, General Electric, and American missions in Asia. Its dense sequence of call signs, frequencies, reception reports, and notes verbales documents both the technical problem of an overcrowded international spectrum and the political importance attached to American shortwave broadcasting. The final sheets also capture a striking wartime transition from efforts to protect American signals and improve their news content to monitoring and potentially jamming Japanese broadcasts aimed at Latin America.
